Frederick stared at the glowing runes, the weight of eternity pressing against his mortal heart. The draft from the hidden chamber seemed to whisper warnings, the very air thick with the scent of ozone and ancient dust. He looked at the list of ingredients—rare herbs, moonlight captured in crystal, and a drop of his own blood. The power to live forever was within his grasp, but the cost was the loss of everything that made life precious: its fragility, its urgency, its end.

He thought of his wife, Elara, whose laughter had been the soundtrack of his youth, now silenced by time. He thought of his children, grown and scattered, their lives vibrant precisely because they were fleeting. To choose immortality would be to become a statue in a museum of his own making, watching the world change while he remained static, a ghost in a living body.

With a trembling hand, Frederick did not reach for the vial. Instead, he reached for the edge of the parchment. He held it over the brazier, the flames licking at the corners. The runes flared in protest, a low hum vibrating through the stone floor, but Frederick’s resolve was unshaken. He watched as the ink curled and blackened, the secrets of eternal life dissolving into ash.

As the last page turned to cinders, the draft ceased. The chamber fell silent, save for the crackle of the fire. Frederick felt a profound lightness, not of the body, but of the soul. He had chosen mortality, and in doing so, he had reclaimed his humanity. He turned and walked out of the chamber, leaving the altar empty, ready to return to the world of the living, where every moment was a gift precisely because it could not last.

***

The explorer who reached America in 1492 was Christopher Columbus.
